newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Big bad U.S. payrolls are back again.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Big bad U.S. payrolls are back again.

text.p: U.S. payrolls, the most avidly watched economic figure in the world, will set financial markets alight once more this week, economists said.

The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) on Tuesday and housing figures on Thursday will act as warm-up acts before the jobs data on Friday. Markets are already nervous about the chance of higher U.S. interest rates and the coming data are seen as decisive.
Europe also has a big week with a cocktail of growth, production and jobs data out of Germany, France and Britain.
"Payrolls loom largest," said Brian Venables, analyst at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
He said the NAPM and housing completions -- especially after a recent surge in new home sales -- would be crucial as well.

If the reports combined to show a vibrant economy, a Federal Reserve rate rise at a September Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting will be back on the agenda, he said. "The one thing the Fed will try to avoid is a fiasco like we had in July," Venables said. In July, the Fed left rates unchanged at a FOMC meeting but markets were spooked when subsequent data showed plenty of economic muscle.
"The advantage this time is the FOMC is after the data rather than before," Venables said.
Simon Briscoe, economist at Nikko Europe in London, said payrolls would set the tone for bond markets.
"If you plot a chart of the long bond yield, the five or six lurches all occurred on payroll day," he said. He forecast a 225,000 rise compared with a 193,000 rise in July.
France reports second quarter gross domestic product (GDP) on Wednesday and Germany will do likewise on Thursday, the same day it releases unemployment numbers.
"German unemployment will probably be of some interest," said Steve Englander, economist at Smith Barney in Paris.

Analysts said evidence of a strengthening economy in the jobs figures, and decent growth in the second quarter, would lead many to suspect the Bundebank's August repo rate cut was the last rate reduction in the current cycle.
Signs of economic life in Germany would also boost the mark and lead to tension in other European markets, they said.
"Anything that raises that kind of speculation would be bad for the best of Europe," Englander said.
In France, markets were likely to be cheered if GDP was a bit more upbeat, although analysts did not expect it would be.

"Basically the big negative is any speculation they're not going to get into EMU. The big risk is the deficit overshoot and signs of growth means the government may actually collect tax revenues," Englander said.

Britain has industrial production numbers on Friday, but before that it will be preoccupied with a regular meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Eddie George on Wednesday.

"I am personally expecting another rate cut, but not as soon as next week," Briscoe said. Venables said he saw as much as a 50-50 chance of a rate cut on the view the ruling Conservative Party will want to start priming the pump early ahead of the next British general election.
Briscoe said the British output numbers would be key.

"There's a lot of interest in what is happening in manufacturing," he said. "It looks as though the trough has now passed and manufaturers are getting back into control by cutting staff and cutting stocks."
Japan has a less exciting time ahead of them after a busy week which featured the Bank of Japan "tankan" report, analysts said, with no major figures expected to give markets a shake.
